title: Defending the Faith
lead: An apology (Greek apologia, 'a speech in defense') is a reasoned answer for the faith. The Bible calls believers to 'speak in your defense' of their hope (1 Peter 3:15), shows Paul defending himself and the gospel before crowds, councils and kings, and early Christian writers called the Apologists, such as Aristides and Justin, addressed emperors and educated pagans. The Epistle to Diognetus, of uncertain date, answers one educated inquirer.

sections.b: 1 Peter tells believers under pressure: 'Be ready, always, to speak in your defense when anyone asks you to account for the hope that is in you. But do it gently and with fear' (1 Peter 3:15). The Greek apologia was a speech made in court. Paul uses it of his own answers: 'listen to me as I now give you my defense' (Acts 22:1), 'This is my defense to those who question me' (1 Corinthians 9:3), 'as I defend the good news' (Philippians 1:7), 'The first time I made my defense, nobody came to my side' (2 Timothy 4:16). Colossians adds the manner: words that 'come with grace and have salt in them' (Colossians 4:6).
sections.refs: 1 Peter 3:15; Acts 22:1; Acts 26:2; 1 Corinthians 9:3; Philippians 1:7; Philippians 1:16; 2 Timothy 4:16; Colossians 4:6

sections.b: The Bible's two speeches to pagans show the pattern later apologists followed. At Lystra Paul calls the crowd to turn from 'empty things to the God who lives, who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them' (Acts 14:15), and says God 'did not leave himself without a witness' (Acts 14:17). At Athens he starts from an altar 'To an unknown god', quotes their poets, argues that God needs nothing from human hands and is not like 'gold or silver or stone', and ends with the coming judgment and the resurrection (Acts 17:22-31).

Early Christian writers addressed defenses to emperors and to the educated. Aristides' Apology is headed as 'the defense which Aristides the philosopher made before Hadrian the King' and begins with a greeting to the emperor and divides humankind into 'four classes of men in this world:— Barbarians and Greeks, Jews and Christians' (Apology 2, Ante-Nicene Fathers). Justin Martyr's First Apology, addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons, argued that idols are 'soulless and dead' (9), that 'God does not need the material offerings which men can give' (10), and that Christians do not expose their children (27, 29). Lake says the Epistle to Diognetus 'resembles the apology of Aristides, and somewhat less closely those of Justin and Tatian'.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 2:1-10; Epistle to Diognetus 3:3-5; Epistle to Diognetus 5:6

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus addresses no emperor but one inquirer, 'most excellent Diognetus', and its date is uncertain: Lake thinks it 'probably later than any of the other writings' among the Apostolic Fathers and reports Harnack's view that it 'more probably belongs to the third than to the second century'. Diognetus had asked what God Christians worship, why they despise death, why they reject the Greek gods and the Jewish observances, what their mutual love is, and why the faith is new (Epistle to Diognetus 1:1). The answer follows the apologists' path: the folly of idols (2), the case against the Jewish sacrifices and customs (3-4), Christians as model citizens whose home is heaven and who hold the world together (5-6), the Word sent by God in forbearance and gentleness, 'for force has no place in God' (Epistle to Diognetus 7:4), the philosophers' errors (8), and God's patience and 'the sweet exchange' (9). It ends not with argument but with an invitation to love and imitate God (10).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 1:1; Epistle to Diognetus 5:1-17; Epistle to Diognetus 6:7; Epistle to Diognetus 7:4; Epistle to Diognetus 10:4-6
